exp.0:0:
It says that this book begins with a message from God, not with an idea of Joel's own. The name of God appears at the start, and the verse tells us that the word of the Lord came to Joel. Joel is introduced as the son of Pethuel, that is, of Bethuel.

The one speaking is God, and Joel is the messenger who receives the message and passes it on. Nothing more is known about Pethuel, and the verse does not say in what year Joel lived; scholars place him in different periods. What follows shows that the people were living through a very great calamity, and God wanted them to listen carefully.

For today: before looking for what I think, I can open the Bible humbly and ask what God is saying to me. His word deserves my attention, even when it makes me uncomfortable or calls me to change.
exp.2:16:
God promises that his people will truly come to know him: "I am the Lord your God," the one who dwells in Zion, his holy mountain. Jerusalem will be holy, that is, set apart for God. The sentence about strangers no longer passing through her means that hostile enemies and foreigners will no longer invade or defile her.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Earlier he announced judgment on the nations and shaking in the heavens and the earth. Now he comforts his people: in the midst of all that, he will be their refuge and stronghold. Interpreters differ on whether this is fulfilled in a literal future or in a spiritual way, but all see the promise of restoration.

For today: when everything seems unstable, remember that God is still your refuge. Seek him to know him more, and let his presence give you security and encourage you to live set apart for him.
exp.1:23:
It says there will be abundance after scarcity. The threshing floors are the flat places where the grain was threshed, and they will be full of wheat. The vats were the tubs where grapes and olives were trodden, and they will overflow with wine and oil.

God speaks through the prophet Joel to a people who suffered a terrible plague of locusts that stripped their harvests bare. After calling them to repentance, He promises to restore what was lost. This promise is given within a message of forgiveness and renewal. Some see it only as a material promise for Israel, and others also as an image of spiritual restoration.

For today: if you are going through a loss or a dry season, do not lose hope. Return to God with sincerity, trust His faithfulness, and give thanks now for every provision, for He knows how to restore what seemed lost.
exp.0:13:
It says to proclaim a fast, call a solemn assembly, and gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the Lord your God, to cry out to him. "Proclaim" means to announce aloud. "Call a solemn assembly" means to summon a sacred gathering.

The prophet Joel speaks on God's behalf to a people struck by a terrible plague and drought. The fields and trees have dried up, and there are no longer offerings for the temple. Joel sees this calamity as a serious sign and calls the people, beginning with the priests, to return to God with humility.

For today: when crises or difficulties come, do not face them alone. Seek out your community of faith, set aside time to pray sincerely, and bring your need before God with humility and trust.
exp.1:24:
God promises to give back to his people what they lost. He speaks of "the years that the locust has eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpillar, and the palmerworm," which are different names for insects that devoured the crops. "Restore" means to give back or make good again. God calls this plague "my great army," because he had allowed it or sent it as a correction.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Judah had suffered a terrible plague that left hunger and sorrow. Joel called the people to turn back to God wholeheartedly. Now, in response to their repentance, comes the promise: rain, abundant harvests, and joy. Scholars debate whether the plague was literal, symbolic, or both, but the message of restoration is clear.

For today: if you feel you have lost years through mistakes or through pain, return to God with sincerity. He can heal and renew your life, though not always in the way you expect.
exp.1:12:
It says that God does not want only outward signs of sorrow, but a true change within. Where the source uses an old word for tearing, the verse here speaks of rending your heart, and the idea is that tearing one's clothes was a custom of grief, yet what is asked here is a heart truly broken. The word for turning back is simply turning back to God. And the phrase about God relenting from the punishment shows that God would rather forgive than punish.

The prophet Joel speaks, announcing the word of the Lord. The people were facing a judgment that was near, described as the day of the Lord, and probably a great plague of locusts. God calls them to return to him with fasting, weeping, and prayer. Scholars debate details of the date and the exact setting, but the call is clear.

For today: it is not enough to carry out rituals or to look religious. When you fail, come to God sincerely, acknowledge your wrong, and change what you need to change. He is patient and compassionate, and he receives you with mercy.
exp.2:6:
God says he will bring his people back from the distant places where they were sold as slaves. He will also punish those who sold them, making the same thing happen to them that they did to others. "I will return your recompense upon your own head" means they will receive back the harm they caused.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. The neighboring nations had plundered Judah's treasure and sold its children to the Greeks, to take them far from their land. God presents himself as the defender of his people and a just judge. Scholars debate which exact events the passage refers to.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. If you have been mistreated, you can trust that he will bring justice, so there is no need for you to take revenge. And if you have harmed someone, this is a call to correct yourself and ask for forgiveness.
exp.1:15:
God calls the whole people to gather in a solemn way, set apart for Him. No one is left out: elders, children, and even the infants still nursing. Even newlyweds must leave their room and their marriage bed to join the assembly. Setting the gathering apart means treating it as something holy.

The prophet Joel speaks to Judah in the face of a serious crisis, described earlier as a plague of locusts and as a day of the Lord that is drawing near. For this reason he calls for fasting, repentance, and crying out for forgiveness. A bridegroom would normally be excused from duties, so this call shows the urgency: nothing is more important than turning back to God.

For today: when there is pain, guilt, or need, do not face it alone. Seek out your family and your church, and pray together, setting aside comfort and busy schedules.
exp.1:10:
The Lord himself raises his voice at the head of his army, like a commander giving orders. That army is vast and powerful, and it carries out whatever God commands. The words "camps" and "troops" refer to the army's encampments or companies. "Endure" here means to bear up under or withstand. The closing question shows that no one can stand through that day by their own strength.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah. A plague of locusts was coming, and a greater threat called "the day of the Lord." Some think the army is the locusts, others think it is enemy troops, and others think it is both. What matters is that God rules over them. And right after this, in the verses that follow, God calls the people to repentance.

Today we can take God seriously without living in fear. If something in your life is pulling you away from him, do not wait any longer: return to him sincerely, because he is merciful and ready to forgive.
exp.1:19:
God says he will drive the enemy far away from you, the one described as coming from the north, and force him into a land that is dry and empty. His troops will be split up: the front part toward the eastern sea (probably the Dead Sea) and the rear part toward the western sea (the Mediterranean). There they will rot away, and their terrible stench will rise up. The rest of the verse says the enemy has done great things, which is understood as the enemy's arrogance, though some interpret that phrase differently.

The prophet Joel speaks for God. Judah had suffered a devastating plague of locusts, which the prophet presents as a sign of judgment. Many see the one "from the north" as that plague or as a future army; it is interpreted in several ways. God responds to his people's repentance with forgiveness and restoration.

For today: when you feel that an enormous problem threatens you, remember that God can remove it and also restore what has been lost. Come to him sincerely and trust in his care.
exp.2:7:
It says that God himself will repay the enemies of Judah in kind. Their sons and daughters will be handed over to the people of Judah, and these will sell them to the Sabeans, a people far away. "Far off" means distant. The Sabeans were people from the south of Arabia, known for trade. The phrase "for the Lord hath spoken it" stresses that this is a sure word.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Tyre, Sidon and Philistia had sold inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem as slaves, handing them over to the Greeks. God responds with justice: what they did will come back upon them.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. We do not have to take revenge; we can trust that he will do justice in his time. And it reminds us to treat people with dignity, never as merchandise.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the trumpet (in Hebrew, the shofar) should be sounded in Zion, God's holy mountain, to give a warning. The word for "sound an alarm" means to make a loud public announcement. "Tremble" expresses a serious fear of what is coming. "The day of the Lord" is a time when God acts in judgment, and the text says it is very near.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Joel, to Judah. The trumpet was the signal of alarm at a time of danger. The verses that follow describe a huge army, and many understand this as a plague of locusts, others as an invading army, and some see both. The purpose of the warning is to call the people to turn back to God.

For today: do not wait until a crisis arrives to draw near to God. If He shows you something you need to correct, respond to Him with humility and without delay, because His warning is a sign of His mercy.
exp.1:21:
God tells the animals of the field not to be afraid. The pastures of the wilderness will become green again, the trees will bear fruit, and the fig tree and the vine will produce abundantly.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Earlier, a great plague and a drought had left the land ruined, and even the animals suffered. God promises to remove the one who comes from the north, an enemy force; some think these are locusts, others an army. Interpreters explain this in several ways. Then he announces restoration for the land and for his people.

For today: when everything seems dry and without hope, you can trust that God cares for what he has created and knows how to restore it. Give him your fears and wait with gratitude, while faithfully doing what is yours to do.
exp.2:3:
God speaks to Tyre, Sidon, and the regions of the Philistines (the "Palestine" of this version). He asks them what they have against Him, and whether what they are after is revenge on Him. He warns that if they do this, He will soon return the same harm upon their own heads. The phrase about return means that they will receive what they deserve.

The Lord speaks in the middle of His announcement of judgment on the nations. These peoples had plundered the treasure of Judah, sold its people as slaves, and handed over its children. By harming God's people, they were in the end offending Him. The text does not detail every historical fact, but it makes the charge clear.

For today: God sees injustice, especially against the weak. We do not have to take revenge ourselves; we can trust that He judges with justice. It also reminds us to treat others with respect, because they matter to Him.
exp.1:20:
This verse speaks directly to the land, as if it were a person, and tells it not to be afraid. Instead of fearing, it should be glad and rejoice, because God is going to do great things. The name of God is the LORD, and "rejoice" means to be filled with gladness.

The prophet Joel writes after a terrible plague of locusts that left the fields stripped bare. God promises his people bread, new wine and oil, and also to remove the enemy described as coming from the north. Some understand this to refer to the locusts and others to an army; the Bible does not fully make this clear. The wounded land receives hope of restoration.

For today: if you are going through a loss or a dry season, you can hand your fear over to God. He can restore what was lost. Today, in prayer, name a situation that frightens you and thank him in advance for his faithfulness.
exp.0:8:
It says there is no longer any grain offering or drink offering for the temple. Without harvests, the priests have nothing to bring, and that is why they are in mourning.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah after a terrible plague of locusts that swept through fields, vineyards and fig trees. The exact date of the book is unknown. Joel presents the disaster as a call to return to God. Here the grief reaches the temple, because worship depended on what the land produced.

For today: when we lose something we take for granted, such as work, health or resources, we can stop and bring that pain honestly to God. Losses can turn our hearts toward Him, who remains our provision.
exp.1:18:
God answers the cry of his people. He promises to send them grain, new wine (must), and oil, which were the staple foods of the land, and says they will be satisfied. He also promises that he will never again leave them in disgrace, that is, in shame and mockery, in the sight of the other nations.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Joel. Earlier, a plague of locusts and a severe drought had laid waste the fields, and the prophet called the people to fast and to return to God with humility. This verse is the divine answer: when people repent, God shows compassion and restores.

For today: when you feel ruined or ashamed, come to God with sincerity. He listens, cares for your needs, and knows how to restore your dignity. Trust that his mercy is greater than your failure.
exp.1:30:
It says that before the day of the Lord comes, the sun will be darkened and the moon will take on the color of blood. It is language of signs in the sky. "Terrible" means that it causes fear and awe.

The prophet Joel speaks, announcing what God said. Earlier, God promised to pour out his Spirit on everyone, including male and female servants. Then come signs and judgment. But the next verse offers hope: whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Some understand these signs literally, others as symbolic language; Christians also connect this with Pentecost (Acts 2).

For today: do not live in fear or try to guess dates. Instead, call on God today with sincerity, trust in his promise of salvation, and live with a prepared heart.
exp.0:2:
This verse is a command: what happened must be told to the children, and they must tell it to their own children, until it reaches the next generation. The word "Tell" here means "relate" or "explain." It is about passing the memory of a very serious event from parent to child.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He has just asked whether anything like this had happened before. What follows describes a plague of locusts that swept through the fields. Scholars debate whether it is a real plague, a symbol of an army, or both. God wants this experience not to be forgotten.

For today: tell your children or others how God has spoken to you, corrected you, or sustained you in difficult times. Your story can teach them to trust God and not to forget his lessons.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that Israel's enemies treated God's people as if they were merchandise. Casting lots meant dividing up people like plunder. They gave a boy in exchange for the services of a prostitute, and they sold girls to obtain wine to drink. It shows a total disregard for human life, using the most vulnerable for their own pleasure.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He announces that when he restores Judah and Jerusalem, he will judge the nations that scattered his people and divided up his land. The valley of Jehoshaphat, a name meaning "the Lord judges," is seen by many as a symbolic place. God defends those who were mistreated.

For today: God sees and takes seriously abuse against children and the defenseless. We can care for, protect, and defend the young people around us, and support those who help them, rather than looking the other way.
exp.2:19:
It says that Judah and Jerusalem will remain inhabited forever, from generation to generation. "Inhabited" here means that people will live there, with a stable and secure life. It is a promise of lasting continuity for God's people.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Joel. Earlier, the text describes a time of blessing: mountains dripping with new wine, milk, and abundant water. It also says that nations such as Egypt and Edom would be judged for their violence against Judah. Many understand this as a promise for Israel; others also see a final fulfillment in the kingdom of God. There is discussion about how exactly it is to be fulfilled. The following verse says that the Lord will dwell in Zion.

For today: even when we see injustice or instability, we can trust that God keeps his promises. His plan does not depend on difficult times, and we can rest in his faithfulness.
exp.1:25:
He says that God will give his people so much food that they will eat until they are fully satisfied. Then they will praise him for the wonderful things he has done for them. The word for being filled to the full is explained as being completely full. Being in a state of disgrace is explained as being humbled or dishonored. God promises that his people will never again go through that kind of shame.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. A devastating plague of locusts had stripped the harvests, and the people went through hunger and humiliation. Many understand the plague as a judgment and a call to repentance. After the people turn back to God, he promises to restore what was lost and to show his care.

For today: if you have experienced losses or failures, you can draw near to God with confidence. He knows how to restore in his own way and in his own time. In the meantime, practice gratitude: acknowledge and give thanks for the good he has already given you.
exp.0:9:
The field is ruined, and the land itself seems to be in mourning. The grain is lost, the new wine (the juice of freshly pressed grapes) has dried up, and the oil has failed. The reader does not need to know any archaic spelling; the verse speaks of the field being wasted, the land mourning, the corn wasted, the new wine dried up, and the oil languishing.

The prophet Joel speaks, sent by God to Judah. He describes a devastating plague, probably of locusts, though some also see it as a picture of a greater judgment. Without harvests there were no offerings for the temple, which is why the priests mourn. Joel calls the people to recognize what is happening and to turn back to God.

For today: when what gave you security falls away, such as your work, your money, or your health, do not hide it. Bring your pain to God honestly, and let that loss draw you closer to Him.
exp.1:4:
It describes this army advancing with a tremendous noise. It sounds like war chariots leaping over the tops of the mountains, like the crackling of a fire that consumes dry stubble. "Dry stubble" refers to the dry remains that burn quickly. "Ready" means prepared. They are like a strong people, ready to fight.

The prophet Joel speaks on behalf of God. He describes a plague of locusts that lays waste to the land, and many believe it also announces a greater judgment, the "day of the LORD." Interpreters differ: some see real locusts, others an army, and others both. The purpose is to awaken the people so that they return to God.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to seek God. He calls us to return to Him sincerely now, because His mercy remains open to those who repent.
exp.0:14:
It says the day of the Lord is very near and will come as ruin sent by God. "Alas for the day!" is a cry of pain and anguish. "Destruction" means total devastation, and "Almighty" is the name that emphasizes God's power.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah. The land is suffering a plague of locusts and a drought that left the fields without a harvest and the temple without offerings. Joel calls the priests and all the people to fast, mourn, and cry out to God. He sees in that calamity a warning of the day of the Lord, when God acts and judges. Interpreters understand it as a present crisis that also announces something greater.

For today: when crises or warnings come, do not ignore them or harden your heart. Stop, acknowledge your need for God, and return to Him sincerely in prayer.
exp.0:1:
It says that the prophet calls the attention of the elders and of all the inhabitants of the land. He asks them whether anything like this had happened in their time or in the time of their ancestors. "Hear" means "listen," and "happened" means "taken place." It is a way of saying: "This is something extraordinary."

Joel, son of Pethuel, speaks and presents his message as the word of the LORD. The verses that follow describe plagues of insects that devastated the fields. It is not known for certain whether Joel is describing real insects, an image of an enemy invasion, or both; scholars interpret it in different ways. What is clear is that he seeks to awaken the people to a serious crisis.

For today: when difficult moments come, let us not overlook them. Let us listen with humility, remember what God has taught, and share with new generations what we learn from Him.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that God will act at a specific time: when he "brings again the captivity" of Judah and Jerusalem. That is, when he returns his people to their land and restores their situation. The word "again" points to a return, and "captivity" refers to the exile of those who were taken away.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Joel. The verse introduces what follows: God will gather the nations and judge them for how they treated his people. Some understand this as something for the end of time, and others see it as an announcement closer to the history of Israel. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God does not forget those who suffer or the injustices that are committed. You can trust that he restores and does justice in his own time. In the meantime, ask him to help you not to take revenge and to treat others with compassion.
exp.1:1:
It says a day is coming that is dark and full of clouds and shadows, like the morning light spreading over the mountains, but here what spreads out is a large and powerful army. "Century" was once an older word meaning "time" or "age"; so there has never been anything like it, nor will there be in all the generations to come.

The prophet Joel speaks on God's behalf to Judah. He commands that the trumpet be sounded to warn the people about the day of the LORD. Many think it describes a real plague of locusts, while others also see a picture of a future judgment or an invading army. Scholars interpret it in different ways. The purpose is to call the people to repentance.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings. Examine your heart today and turn to Him sincerely; His call seeks to restore us, not merely to frighten us.
exp.0:18:
Joel says he will cry out to the Lord, meaning he will ask God for help with urgency. The reason is that the fire and the flame have left the field dry: the pastures of the wilderness, that is, the open grassy areas, and all the trees. Devoured means that it burned away completely.

The prophet Joel speaks to a people struck by a great calamity, pictured as a plague of locusts and a drought. The animals suffer, the harvests are lost, and there is no food. Joel does not stay silent: he sets the example and turns to God. Some think the fire is literal, while others hold that it is a poetic way of speaking about the drought and the damage.

When everything around us dries up or is lost, we can do what Joel did: bring our need to God in sincere prayer, without waiting until everything is resolved.
exp.1:14:
It says that the trumpet should be blown in Zion, the mount where the temple stood in Jerusalem, to warn everyone. To proclaim a fast is to announce publicly that the people will stop eating for a time in order to seek God. To call a solemn assembly is to summon everyone to a sacred gathering.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah. A severe plague of locusts and a drought had devastated the land, and Joel sees it as a sign of God's judgment. Before this verse, he had already called for sincere repentance of the heart, not just outward appearance. Now he asks that everyone gather to cry out to God.

For today: when we face a crisis, we need not carry it alone. We can come together with other believers to pray, repent sincerely, and trust in God's mercy.
exp.2:12:
He says God commands action because the time of judgment has already come. He compares judgment to a harvest: the "sickle" is the tool for reaping, and the "grain" is the ripe crop. The "wine press" is where grapes are trodden, and the "vats" are the tubs where the juice collects. That the vats overflow means wickedness has reached its limit.

Here God speaks through the prophet Joel. He announces that he will judge the nations in the "valley of Jehoshaphat," a name that means "the LORD judges." It is not known for certain whether this is a real place or a symbol. Many see it as an image of the final judgment.

For today: God sees wickedness and will not overlook it. This comforts us when we see injustice, and it invites us to live with humility, seeking his forgiveness and practicing justice.
exp.1:26:
God promises that his people will truly know him. He says that he is in the midst of Israel, that he is the Lord, their only God, and that his people will never again be put to shame, that is, humiliated or left in disgrace before others.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. A terrible plague of locusts had stripped the harvests, and the prophet presents it as a sign of judgment and a call to repentance. If the people turn back to him, God promises to restore what was lost. After this promise comes the announcement of the Spirit poured out on all flesh.

For today: even when you have gone through losses or failures, you can trust that God is present with you. Turn back to him sincerely, and rest in the knowledge that he knows how to restore what was lost, in his own time and his own way.
exp.2:18:
It says Egypt will be destroyed and Edom will become a desolate wilderness. The reason is the mistreatment the people of Judah suffered, because innocent blood was shed in their land. "Desolation" means laid waste, left in ruins. "Violence" here means unjust harm or injury.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Earlier he promises Jerusalem a time of blessing, holiness, and abundance. This verse sets that future against the fate of nations that oppressed Judah. Egypt and Edom appear as examples of hostile peoples. Some see here a literal judgment, others a symbol of God's judgment on all wickedness.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. If you have been wronged, you can bring your pain to him and trust that he will bring justice, without seeking revenge. And examine how you treat others, so that you do not hurt anyone.
exp.1:29:
God announces that he will show extraordinary signs, called "wonders," both in the heavens and on the earth. He mentions blood, fire, and pillars of smoke, images that speak of war, destruction, or judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. First he promises to pour out his Spirit on everyone, regardless of age or position. Then he warns that, before "the great and terrible day of the LORD," there will be signs. Interpreters disagree: some see this in the future, others as already fulfilled in part. Peter quoted this passage at Pentecost (Acts 2).

For today: God gives us an invitation and not just a warning. Even though the world may seem turbulent, "whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be saved." Today you can call on God with confidence and live with hope, not with fear.
exp.0:15:
Joel asks whether it is not true that the food has been cut off before everyone's eyes. Joy and gladness have also been lost from the house of God. "Food" here means nourishment and what sustains life, and "gladness" refers to the festival and the joy of worship.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah after a plague of locusts and a drought. With no harvest, there were no grain or wine offerings for the temple, and the festivals faded. Joel uses this loss to call the people to fast and cry out to God. Some see in this also a warning about the day of the Lord, and it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when something that sustained your life or your joy is missing, do not stay alone in your grief. Bring your loss to God in prayer, and seek to do so together with other believers.
exp.1:2:
This verse describes a huge army advancing like a fire. Everything before it is burned, and behind it only the flame is left. The land that was once beautiful, like the garden of Eden (the garden of Genesis), is turned into a ruined wasteland, that is, a devastated and empty place. No one manages to escape.

The prophet Joel, a messenger of God, speaks and warns Judah that the day of the LORD is coming. Scholars understand this in several ways: a real plague of locusts, an invading army, or both together as a sign of a greater judgment. The purpose is to wake the people so that they return to God, as seen in the rest of the chapter.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings. He speaks to us clearly so that we return to Him before it is too late, and Joel himself reminds us that God is compassionate and forgives those who turn back with their whole heart.
exp.0:5:
It says that an invading nation has entered the land of God. It is very strong and so numerous that it cannot be counted. Its teeth are compared with those of a lion, to show that it devours and destroys everything. The word "nation" here means a people or a nation; the back teeth, the ones that grind, are the cheek teeth.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah. He describes a terrible plague of locusts, and presents it as an army that lays waste to the vineyards and the fig trees. Some think he speaks only of insects; others think he also announces a real army. Joel uses this calamity to call the people to wake up, weep, and turn back to God.

For today: when losses come that we cannot control, let us not ignore them or become distracted. They are an opportunity to stop, pray sincerely, and return to God with humility.
exp.2:15:
What it says: The Lord will speak with force from Jerusalem, roaring like a lion. His voice will make the heavens and the earth tremble. But for those who trust in him, God will be a secure refuge, a firm protection.

Context: The prophet Joel speaks in God's name about the day of the Lord, a time of judgment on the nations that mistreated his people. The valley of decision is an image of the place where God judges. Interpreters differ on how and when this will be fulfilled, but the message is clear: God judges with justice and cares for his own.

For today: When everything around you seems unstable, remember that God remains firm. Today, bring to him in prayer what worries you most, and rest in the fact that he is your refuge.
exp.2:4:
God accuses Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistine regions. He says they took his silver, his gold, and his precious and beautiful things, and placed them in their temples. The phrase "you have taken" means that they seized them. "Temples" here refers to the places of their gods; it can also be understood as palaces, and scholars interpret it in both ways.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. Judah and Jerusalem had been plundered, and their people sold as slaves to the Greeks. God takes this as an offense against Himself, because Judah is his people. He promises to judge those who did it and to repay them with what they sowed. It is not known with certainty which invasion the text refers to.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. If today you have something that does not belong to you, or you have benefited from others, return it and act with honesty. And if someone has wronged you, trust that God is just.
exp.1:13:
This verse expresses a humble hope. The question "who knows whether he will return?" means that God could change his mind, show compassion, and lift the punishment. If he does, he would leave a blessing behind him: harvests and provision. The grain offering was a gift of grain, and the drink offering was wine poured out. Both were presented to God in the temple.

Here the prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah in the middle of a serious crisis, described as a plague of locusts and a day of the Lord. God himself calls them to turn back to him with their whole heart, not merely with outward gestures. Scholars disagree about the exact date of the book. The phrase "who knows?" shows that no one can demand anything from God, but one can trust in his merciful character.

For today: when you have failed or are facing a difficult situation, come to God with sincerity, without excuses or pretense. Trust that he is merciful, even though you do not control the outcome.
exp.0:11:
It says the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, the palm, the apple tree and all the trees of the field dried up. With them, the people's joy also dried up. "Dried up" is the meaning of the word for this, and the words that mean "perished" or "died" have the sense of being lost. The "apple tree" may refer to another similar fruit, since experts are not sure which tree it was.

Joel, a prophet of God, speaks to Judah after a devastating plague, probably of locusts (1:4), though some also see it as a symbol of a greater judgment. The harvests were lost, and even worship in the temple was left without offerings. Joel calls farmers and priests to mourn and to seek God with fasting and prayer.

For today: when our sources of joy dry up, such as work, health or money, we can bring that loss to God in prayer, instead of keeping it silent or becoming hardened.
exp.2:10:
It says that the neighboring nations must assemble and come, and that God himself brings down his "mighty ones," that is, his warriors or powerful angels. "Assemble yourselves" and "gather yourselves together" mean to come together; the "heathen" are the nations that are not Israel; "Lord" is the name of God.

Here the prophet Joel speaks. The nations had mistreated Israel, and God announces judgment on them in the valley of "Jehoshaphat," a name meaning "the Lord judges." The verses before this one reverse the famous call to beat swords into plowshares. Many see here an image of the final judgment; others connect it to a judgment in history. Scholars debate which reading is correct.

For today: God sees wickedness and does not overlook it. We can trust that he will do justice, so there is no need to take revenge; rather, let us live with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.0:7:
It says the people should mourn with a very deep grief, like a young woman who is betrothed or newly married and who puts on mourning clothes made of rough cloth, because she has lost the husband of her youth. A young woman is a girl in the bloom of her youth.

The prophet Joel speaks to Judah after a terrible plague of locusts, which he describes as an army with lions' teeth. They stripped vineyards, fig trees and fields, and even took away the offerings at the temple. Joel uses this image of sudden loss to call the people to recognize the seriousness of the moment and return to God. Some think the plague also announces a greater judgment.

For today: do not rush to minimize your pain or that of others. Facing a loss, it is healthy to weep sincerely and to bring that grief to God, who listens to us and can comfort and renew us.
exp.1:7:
It says this army advances in perfect order: no one pushes or gets in the way of their companion, and each one follows his own course (the word for "course" here means path or direction). Even when they throw themselves onto the weapons, they are not wounded, meaning nothing can stop them.

Joel, a prophet of God, speaks to the people of Judah. He describes a terrible plague of locusts as if it were an army, to warn that the "day of the LORD" is drawing near. Some believe he is speaking only of real locusts; others believe he also foretells an enemy army. Soon, in the same chapter, God calls them to return to him with all their heart.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to draw near to God. If you sense that he is calling you to correct something, respond today with humility and sincere prayer.
exp.1:28:
It says God will pour out his Spirit also on the male servants and the female servants, that is, on those who were slaves or served others. "Pour out" shows something abundant, not scarce. "In those days" refers to the future time that God announces.

God speaks through the prophet Joel to Israel, after calling them to repentance and promising them restoration. The promise includes sons, daughters, elders, young men, and servants, leaving out no one of lower social standing. In Acts 2, Peter quotes this passage and says it was fulfilled at Pentecost. Some believers see a complete fulfillment there, and others think something is still yet to be fulfilled.

For today: no one is too humble or insignificant for God. If you belong to him, ask him to guide you by his Spirit, and treat everyone with respect, because God shows no distinction.
exp.0:17:
This verse describes the suffering of the animals. The beasts groan, the herds of cattle are confused, and the flocks of sheep are ruined, because there is no pasture.

The prophet Joel is speaking, and he describes a great disaster in Judah: a plague of locusts and a drought that swept through the fields. There is no longer any harvest, no food for the people, and no offerings for the temple. Joel points out that even the animals suffer, and so he calls the people to cry out to God. Scholars debate whether he is describing a historical event, a vivid image, or both.

For today: our choices and our crises also affect those who have no voice. We can care with compassion for animals and for creation, and bring our needs and the needs of others before God in prayer.
exp.1:11:
This verse is a call from God to his people: "turn ye even to me with all your heart." The word that is rendered "turn" means to turn around and come back to God. The phrase "with weeping, and with mourning" speaks of deep sorrow over sin, and fasting was a way of showing humility and a need for God.

The one speaking is God himself, through the prophet Joel. Earlier, he has described the day of the Lord as something very serious and frightening, with a great plague and a judgment near at hand. Even so, God does not begin with punishment alone, but with an invitation: "Therefore also now." There is still time to return. The verses that follow say that God is merciful, slow to anger, and great in kindness.

For today: it is not enough to carry out outward rituals. If there is something that keeps you away from God, bring it honestly before him, acknowledge it, and return to him with all your heart. He welcomes the one who comes back.
exp.1:27:
God promises that, after restoring his people, he will pour out his Spirit on "all flesh," that is, on every kind of person. Sons and daughters will speak on God's behalf (they will prophesy), the old will dream dreams, and the young men will see visions.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He has just promised Israel that he will remove the plague and the drought, and that his people will no longer be put to shame. Then he announces something greater: his Spirit will be given to everyone, men and women, young and old, even servants. In Acts 2, Peter says this began to be fulfilled at Pentecost. Some believers see a complete fulfillment there, while others expect a fulfillment still to come.

For today: no one is too young, too old, or too ordinary for God to use. Ask him to fill you with his Spirit, and offer yourself to encourage, guide, or serve others.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that the farmers and the vinedressers should be ashamed and weep with loud lamenting, because the wheat and barley harvests have been ruined.

The verse's word "ashamed" means to be put to shame and left confused, so it is rendered here as the sense of being ashamed and dismayed. "Howl" means to cry out in pain. The crop that is ready and about to be gathered is the ripe harvest of the field.

The prophet Joel speaks in God's name to Judah after a devastating plague, described as locusts and drought. With no harvest, there were no longer offerings for the temple, and everyone suffered. Joel uses this calamity to call the people to recognize their situation and turn back to God. Scholars debate whether the plague was literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: when something that sustains your life collapses, do not hide it or ignore it. Allow yourself to feel the pain and bring it honestly to God, trusting that he listens to those who humble themselves before him.
exp.0:12:
It says that the priests and those who serve at the altar must dress in mourning, weep, and cry out in grief. Mourning clothes are what is meant here, and lying the whole night in rough cloth is the sign of penitence. To cry out means to call out loudly. The grain offering is what was presented to God, and the wine offering is what was poured out; there is nothing left in the temple to offer them with.

The prophet Joel speaks in God's name to a people struck by a terrible plague and drought. The fields and the trees dried up, and because of this there was no grain or wine for worship. Joel first calls the priests to lead the people back to God.

For today: when losses or crises come, we should not face them with indifference or with human cleverness alone. We can stop, acknowledge our need, and cry out to God sincerely, and those who lead others should be the first to do so.
exp.2:14:
It says that the sun and the moon will grow dark, and that the stars will stop shining. The phrase about the stars withdrawing their shining means that they will hold back or hide their light. It is an image that something very great is happening across the whole sky.

Here the prophet Joel speaks on behalf of God. He describes the day of the LORD, when God judges the nations for their wickedness. The images of the harvest and the winepress, where grapes are trodden, show a judgment that is ripe and complete. Scholars disagree about whether the darkness is literal, symbolic, or both. But the next verse makes the central point clear: God will be a refuge and a stronghold for his people.

For today: when the world seems dark and unsafe, remember that God is still in control. Trust in him as your refuge, and live in such a way that you do not fear his day.
exp.1:31:
Joel 2:32 says that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Calling on the Lord means asking him for help and trusting in him. Deliverance will be found on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, just as the Lord has said, and it will also be for the remnant, meaning the survivors whom the Lord himself has called. The verse shows that God takes the initiative: it is he who calls.

Joel is the prophet who speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. Before this verse he announces terrible signs that come before the day of the Lord, a time of judgment. But in the middle of that warning he offers hope: God opens a door of salvation. In Acts 2 and Romans 10, the New Testament quotes this verse and applies it to Jesus and the gospel.

For today: when you feel fear, guilt, or uncertainty, call on God simply. You do not need perfect words, only a heart that trusts him.
exp.1:6:
It says that this army advances with impressive strength and order. They run like brave soldiers and climb the wall like men of war. Each one keeps to his own path and does not turn aside from his way. The image shows discipline and determination.

The book of Joel presents the prophet speaking on behalf of God to the people of Judah. It describes a plague of locusts, or an army, or both, since scholars interpret it in different ways. What is certain is that Joel uses this scene to call the people to repentance and to warn them of the day of the LORD.

For today: if these invaders advance without turning aside, how much more can we remain firm on the path of God. Today, choose one concrete decision that brings you closer to Him and do not turn aside from it.
exp.2:8:
This verse is a command addressed to the nations: announce war, call their mightiest warriors to wake up, and let all the fighting men come near. "Proclaim ye this among the Gentiles" means to announce it loudly and publicly, and "Gentiles" refers to the nations. The call to the mighty men is a summons to the warriors to get ready for battle.

It is God who speaks through the prophet Joel. According to the context, He is going to judge the nations that mistreated His people and sold them into slavery. This call to war has an ironic tone: the nations prepare to fight, but they are gathering to be judged. Some see it as a picture of the final judgment, others as a historical event; there are different interpretations.

For today: God sees injustice and does not let it pass. We can trust that He will do justice, so let us leave vengeance in His hands and seek to live with justice and mercy.
exp.2:5:
It says that the people of Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem as slaves to the Grecians. They did this to remove them far from their border.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He defends his people and demands justice for the cruel treatment they received. Those cities took silver, gold, and treasures from God's people, and they trafficked in human beings. God promises that he will bring them back and that the payment for their wickedness will fall on them. Scholars do not agree on the exact date of these events.

For today: God sees injustice, especially when people are treated as merchandise. We can reject all exploitation, defend the vulnerable, and trust that God will bring about justice in his time.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that a huge army invades the city with nothing to stop it. They run along the wall, climb up onto the houses, and enter through the windows like a thief, that is, like a thief who slips in where no one expects.

Joel is the prophet who speaks in God's name. He describes a terrible invasion, perhaps of locusts or of an army, and many scholars see it as a sign of the day of the Lord. Interpreters do not agree on whether it is a real plague, a human army, or both. The purpose is to wake the people up so that they return to God.

For today: do not put off your return to God. Today you can examine your heart, ask for forgiveness, and trust in Him again with sincerity.
exp.2:9:
It says that the peoples must turn their field tools into weapons. Hoes (for digging the ground) and sickles (for cutting wheat) would become swords and spears. Even the weak are encouraged to say: "I am strong."

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He calls the nations that mistreated his people to prepare for war, and gathers them to the valley of Jehoshaphat, where he will judge them. It is a picture of judgment, not a permission to fight. It is the opposite of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, where weapons become tools of peace.

For today: when the world exalts strength and violence, remember that God is the final judge. Trust Him instead of seeking revenge, and use your hands to build and to serve.
exp.2:13:
It says that great multitudes of peoples are gathered in the "valley of decision," and that the day of the Lord is already near. The word "decision" here refers to a sentence or verdict, not a personal choice. In the Hebrew, the term suggests something decided or pronounced by a judge.

The prophet Joel describes a judgment of God on the nations that mistreated his people. God himself speaks in the preceding verses and announces that he will judge them for their great wickedness. The name of the valley means "the Lord judges"; it is not known for certain whether it is a real place or a symbolic name. Even so, the passage ends with hope: God will be a refuge and a stronghold for his people.

For today: God sees injustice and has the final word. This invites us to trust in him instead of taking revenge, and to live each day ready to give account to him, taking refuge in his mercy.
exp.1:3:
It says this army looks like horses, and that it advances at full speed, like horsemen in the middle of a charge. The word for appearance here means the look or aspect of something. The phrase for the horsemen refers to riders or cavalry.

The prophet Joel speaks on behalf of God and warns Judah of a day of the Lord that is coming near. He describes a devastating plague of locusts, though many believe it also points to an invading army; scholars interpret it in different ways. Locusts do in fact have a head that resembles that of a horse. The image is meant to awaken the people so that they will turn back to God.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to arrive before we seek God. Joel invites us to return to Him with our whole heart (Joel 2:12-13), because He is compassionate and slow to anger. Today we can set aside a few minutes to pray and put in order whatever separates us from Him.
exp.2:11:
It says that God calls the nations to wake up and go up to the valley of Jehoshaphat. There God himself will sit as judge to judge all the surrounding peoples. The "heathen" are the nations, and "round about" means the ones that surround Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Joel. The nations had mistreated his people, and God announces that he will call them to account. The name Jehoshaphat means "the Lord judges," and it is not certain that it is an exact geographical place; many understand it as a symbolic place of God's judgment. The following verse calls it "the valley of decision."

For today: God sees every injustice, and one day he will judge it with perfect justice. Because of this we do not need to take revenge. We can trust him, do good, and live with humility, remembering that we too need his mercy.
exp.2:17:
It says that when God restores his people, there will be an enormous abundance. "New wine" is fresh grape juice, and the hills are the high ground. The mountains will drip with sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, and the streams of Judah will run with water. Furthermore, a fountain will come out of the temple and water the valley of the acacias, which was a dry area; its exact location is not certain.

The prophet Joel speaks, announcing what God will do. Before this, God judges the nations and protects his people. Then comes this picture of peace, with God dwelling in Zion. Some understand it as a promise for Israel, others as a spiritual picture of God's kingdom, and others see both.

For today: when you go through dry seasons, remember that God is the source of life. Seek him in prayer and in his Word, and trust that he will fulfill his promises.
exp.1:9:
It says that when this army arrives, the earth will tremble and the heavens will shake. The sun and the moon will grow dark, and the stars will stop shining. "They will withhold their brightness" means that they will pull back or hide their light.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah, who face either a plague of locusts or an invading army (interpreters understand it in different ways). Joel presents this as a sign of the day of the LORD, a time of judgment. The language of the darkened sky expresses the seriousness of the moment, and God calls the people to return to Him.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. When something shakes your life, use it as a call to draw near to Him with sincerity, praying and asking for forgiveness, rather than hardening your heart.
exp.2:1:
God says that he will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat. There he will judge them for what they did to his people Israel: they scattered them among other countries and divided up their land.

God speaks through the prophet Joel. He has just promised to restore Judah and Jerusalem after their captivity. Now he announces that he will set right the injustices committed against his people. Jehoshaphat means "the Lord judges," and it is not known for certain whether it is a geographical place or a symbolic name; there are different interpretations.

For today: God sees every injustice and does not forget it. We can rest in the knowledge that he will judge with perfect justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. Let us hand our wounds over to God, and seek to treat others with justice and compassion.
exp.0:16:
This verse describes a ruined harvest. The seed rotted under the clods, that is, under the dry and hardened ground. The supplies are the stores of food, and the barns are the storehouses or granaries where the grain was kept. Everything was left empty or destroyed, because the wheat had withered.

Joel, a prophet of Judah, speaks to the people in the middle of a severe calamity, described with locusts, drought and fire. He sees in it a warning: the day of the LORD is near. Without a harvest, there were no longer offerings for the temple, and the joy of God's house was fading. Scholars debate whether the locusts are literal or symbolic, but the call is clear: return to God.

For today: when what seemed secure collapses, that is a good moment to cry out to God and remember that our true trust is not in full barns, but in Him.
exp.0:4:
The verse tells the drunkards to wake up and weep, and to howl, all you who drink wine, because the new wine, the sweet juice just pressed from the grapes that later becomes wine, has been taken away from your mouths. That is, the wine you enjoyed is gone.

The prophet Joel speaks on behalf of God to Judah. A plague of insects devastated the fields, the vineyards, and the fig trees. Without grapes there is no wine. Joel begins with those who live dazed by drink, so that they will open their eyes to the tragedy. Some think the plague is real, and others think it also symbolizes an invading army; the text allows both readings.

Today: let us not wait until we have lost everything before we wake up. If something puts us to sleep, such as alcohol, entertainment, or any pleasure, let us ask God to help us live alert and to turn back to Him.
exp.0:3:
It says that a plague of insects came in waves, one after another. What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the bush locust devoured; and what remained, the destroyer consumed. These are four names of insects that destroy crops, and scholars are not sure which exact species each one refers to. Some believe they are stages of the same locust, while others think they are different plagues.

The prophet Joel speaks to the people of Judah. He asks them to remember this great devastation, which they will tell to their children and grandchildren. Some think it is a real plague; others believe it also announces a greater judgment.

For today: when everything seems to be slowly lost, do not ignore it. Stop, acknowledge the situation, and seek God with humility, because He invites us to return to Him.
exp.1:16:
This verse asks that the priests, who served God in the temple, weep between the porch and the altar, that is, between the temple porch and the altar of sacrifices. They are to plead: "Spare thy people, O Lord." They ask that his heritage, the people who belong to him, not be given over to reproach or be made to rule over by other nations, who would mockingly say: "Where is their God?"

Joel, the prophet, speaks in the middle of a serious crisis, described earlier as a plague of locusts and a threat of judgment. He calls the whole people to fast and gather, and asks the leaders to intercede. Afterward, God responds with compassion: he cares for his land, forgives, and restores provision.

For today: when we fail, we can come to God with sincere humility, without excuses, and also pray for others. He receives with mercy anyone who turns to him with all their heart.
exp.1:5:
It says that, before this advancing army, the peoples are filled with fear. The source's "they will fear" is rendered here as "they shall be much pained," which matches the verse your reader sees. The phrase about faces growing pale, sad and lifeless like a withered plant means that the faces grow pale and dark with distress. It is the reaction of someone who sees something coming that they cannot stop.

The prophet Joel, sent by God to Judah, speaks here. He describes an invasion, perhaps of locusts or of an army, and scholars understand it in different ways. Whatever it was, Joel presents it as "the day of the LORD," a serious sign for the people to recognize their sin and return to God. Later in this same chapter, God invites them to repentance and promises mercy.

For today: when fear paralyzes you, do not simply stand and stare at the problem. Return to God sincerely, for he is the one who offers forgiveness, comfort and hope.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that even the wild animals, who do not reason as we do, cry out to God in desperation. The word "cry out" means they call out loudly, the way someone pleads for help. "Pastures" are the grasslands, the fields of grass. The streams dried up and the fire burned the pastures of the wilderness, that is, the open lands where the animals roamed.

The one speaking is the prophet Joel, who has just said, "To you, O Lord, I will cry." He describes a serious calamity in Judah, with a plague of locusts and drought, which left the people and the animals without food. Joel uses this image to call the people to turn back to God. Some think the "fire" is a way of speaking of the scorching drought; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when everything dries up around you, do not stay silent. Cry out to God sincerely, even if all that comes out is groaning, because He hears.
exp.2:20:
God promises to cleanse blood that he had not cleansed before. Scholars understand the first sentence in two ways: God will bring justice for the innocent blood that was shed, or God will forgive the guilt of his people. What is certain is the ending: the Lord will dwell in Zion.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Joel. The verses before this one announce punishment for nations such as Egypt and Edom, which harmed Judah. Then God promises that Judah will be inhabited forever. This verse closes the book with hope: God sets right the injustice and stays with his people.

For today: when you feel that an injustice has gone unanswered, bring it to God in prayer. He sees, he judges with justice, and he wants to be near you. Trust him and refrain from taking revenge yourself.
exp.1:22:
Here the prophet invites God's people, the children of Zion, to be filled with joy in the Lord. The reason is that God gave them the early rain in its proper measure and at its proper time, and he promises to send again both the early and the late rain, the autumn and spring rains, as in the best of times.

Joel writes after a terrible plague of locusts and a drought that destroyed the crops. After calling the people to repentance, the prophet announces that God will respond with restoration. The verses that follow speak of abundant harvests and of years restored.

For today: when we go through loss, we can trust that God is faithful and knows how to restore. Today you can thank him for something specific he has already given you, and wait patiently for what is still to come.
exp.0:6:
It says that an invading nation, compared to locusts or an army, destroyed God's vine and fig tree. It stripped off their bark, left them without leaves, and threw down their branches, which were left white and dry. The word "laid waste" means ruined completely; "barked" means that the bark was stripped away.

The prophet Joel speaks, calling the land of God "my vine" and "my fig tree." He describes a terrible calamity that left Judah without a harvest, without wine, and without offerings for the temple. Scholars debate whether the plague is real locusts, an army, or both. Joel uses that tragedy to call the people to wake up and return to God.

For today: when something we care for deeply is lost, we do not have to keep silent about the pain. We can grieve it honestly before God, examine our hearts, and return to him, trusting that he is still our refuge.
exp.1:17:
Joel 2:18 says that the Lord will be jealous for his land and pity his people. This verse says that God will "be jealous" for his land, meaning he cares for it with a zealous love, like someone who will not tolerate harm to what he loves. He also "will pity" his people. This is God's response after the people repented.

The prophet Joel speaks in a time of great crisis, with a plague of locusts and a drought that ruined the fields. Joel called everyone, from the elders to newlyweds, to fast and pray. The priests wept, asking for mercy. This verse marks the turning point: God responds with compassion. Scholars debate whether the plague was literal, symbolic, or both, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you have failed or are going through a difficult time, do not stay hidden. Return to God sincerely, for he moves with love toward those who repent.

sum.2: God promises to restore Judah and Jerusalem, and to judge the nations that mistreated and sold off his people, calling them to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. That day will be one of trembling, but God will be a refuge and stronghold for Israel. Afterward there will be abundant blessing, and the LORD will dwell in Zion forever.
sum.1: Joel announces the day of the LORD as a terrifying army that is coming, but God calls his people to turn back to him with all their heart, because he is merciful and slow to anger. If they repent, God promises to restore what was lost, to remove the invader, and to pour out his Spirit on all people. Whoever calls on his name will be saved.
sum.0: Joel announces a terrible plague of locusts that destroyed the fields, the vineyards, and the trees, leaving the people and the animals without food. He calls the priests and all the people to mourn, fast, and cry out to God, because the day of Jehovah is near.
